description: Cosmic Minds is a team of curious thinkers and creative innovators passionate about space exploration. We combine imagination, scientific thinking, and teamwork to design engaging space missions and tackle challenges beyond Earth. Driven by curiosity and a spirit of innovation, we aim to transform bold ideas into meaningful possibilities and explore new frontiers, one mission at a time.
summary:
What did we develop?
We developed HANDOVER, a browser-based space mission design and calibration game where you never fly your own spacecraft. As the Architect, you design a lunar orbiter (such as our baseline Astraquill configuration) under strict mass, power, and budget constraints, inspect uncertainty fog ranges, declare six engineering assumptions with confidence sliders (50%–99%), buy up to three verification tests, and write a strict 200-word Handover Document. Another player—via a shareable Base64 Handover Code—or a rule-based AI Operator then flies 12 operations turns seeing only that document against a hidden, deterministic Reality Engine.
How does it address the challenge?
HANDOVER turns systems engineering into interactive gameplay by uniting real aerospace trade-offs (rocket equation, solar/eclipse energy, thermal, radiation, and link budgets) with risk communication. A post-flight Mission Court traces anomalies through a causal blame graph and scores epistemic calibration alongside mission science.
Why is it important?
Real missions like Mars Climate Orbiter failed from overconfidence and ambiguous handovers. HANDOVER teaches players to quantify uncertainty and document limits clearly.
details:
HANDOVER: Build a spacecraft someone else can fly.

HANDOVER is a browser-based space mission design and calibration game. Most space games test whether a player can build a spacecraft. HANDOVER tests whether the player knows what they do not know, and whether they can pass that knowledge to someone else.

How it works. There are three ways to play:

  • Architect Mode: The player selects a target mission (Lunar Orbiter, with Mars Orbiter as an extended option) and assembles 9 spacecraft subsystems under a strict budget. They inspect “uncertainty fog” around each subsystem, declare 6 engineering assumptions with confidence sliders (50%–99%), and choose from 4 verification tests under a 3-turn schedule cap to narrow uncertainty. They then write a strict 200-word Handover Document with explicit units on every limit. The Lunar Orbiter scenario is modeled on a 100 km low lunar orbit with a 118-minute period, a 40-minute nominal eclipse, a 20% dry mass margin, and a 1361 W/m² solar constant.
  • Operator Mode: The Architect’s design is packed into a Base64 Handover Code (HO1:...). A teammate pastes the code and flies 12 operations turns while seeing only the 200-word document and up to 3 Q&A answers. They face the exact seeded “Reality Engine” truth, just as a real operations team inherits a spacecraft.
  • Ghost Partner Play: Solo players fly one of three prebuilt Ghost Architect packages—Artemis Minimalist (balanced, well-documented), Icarus Express (high risk, flawed handover with a unit-discipline trap), and Aegis Heavy (heavy thermal and power management)—or hand their own design to a deterministic AI Operator.

A deterministic Reality Engine with an optional “Murphy Mode” (which shifts the Architect’s lowest-confidence assumptions adversely) reveals how the design performs across 4 mission events (long eclipse season, solar particle flare, star tracker dropout, and DSN comms dropout). Brier Calibration Scoring (100 × (1 − Brier)) and an interactive Mission Court blame graph trace any anomaly back to an assumption, a skipped test, a documentation/units gap, or an operator mistake. The app also includes Aerospace Learn Cards, a local Heritage Log of flown parts, and a NASA Figures reference.

Benefits. Players practice stating assumptions honestly, matching confidence to evidence, deciding which verification tests are worth their budget and schedule cost, and writing concise, unambiguous handovers. Unclear handovers and overconfident assumptions have contributed to real mission failures—such as the Mars Climate Orbiter’s unit mismatch—and HANDOVER lets players experience that risk safely in about 5 minutes.

Intended impact. It makes systems engineering and flight operations thinking accessible to students, educators, and space enthusiasts while promoting a culture of transparency, unit discipline, and calibrated confidence across engineering teams.

Tools and technology. HANDOVER is a client-side web application with no backend required, built with React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Zustand, and Lucide Icons. It uses a deterministic Mulberry32 seeded random-number generator and truncated normal sampling so every run is reproducible and fair. Handover Codes are Base64-encoded for server-free sharing, and browser localStorage persists the Heritage Log on the player’s device. It incorporates NASA data and case studies including NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) orbital and eclipse parameters, NASA SORCE/TIM Total Solar Irradiance (1361 W/m²), Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO) parameters, the Mars Climate Orbiter Mishap Investigation Board Phase I Report, the Apollo 13 Review Board Report, and the NASA Systems Engineering Handbook (NASA/SP-2016-6105).

Creativity. Rather than rewarding only hardware performance, HANDOVER scores epistemic calibration—penalizing overconfidence and rewarding honest uncertainty. The strict 200-word limit forces engineering prioritization, the unit-trap mechanic turns a historic NASA mishap into playable systems engineering, and the swap-play loop lets players experience the consequences of their own documentation firsthand.

Factors the team considered. Scientific realism, fairness through deterministic seeding, accessibility for non-experts via visual uncertainty fog and Learn Cards, a fast ~5-minute replayable loop, and seamless solo or team play with zero backend dependencies.
